[2022 fall ms math-stat — problem 3]

Two COVID-19 vaccines (A, B) and a control: $n$ observations from group A, $m$ from B, $k$ from control. Overall mean $\mu$, group effects $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$. (1) Write a regression model for the vaccination effects. (2) Give the corresponding model matrix. (3) Can all of $\mu, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$ be estimated? If not, why, and give a fix.

response.text:
Assume \(n,m,k>0\), and let group 1 be vaccine A, group 2 vaccine B, group 3 control. Let

\[
N=n+m+k.
\]

## (1) Regression model

A standard one-way fixed-effects regression/ANOVA model is

\[
Y_{ij}=\mu+\alpha_i+\varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad i=1,2,3,
\]

where

- \(i=1\): vaccine A, \(j=1,\dots,n\),
- \(i=2\): vaccine B, \(j=1,\dots,m\),
- \(i=3\): control, \(j=1,\dots,k\),

and typically

\[
\varepsilon_{ij}\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,\sigma^2)
\]

or at least \(E(\varepsilon_{ij})=0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{ij})=\sigma^2\).

Equivalently, using indicator variables,

\[
Y_\ell=\mu+\alpha_1 I_{\{\ell\in A\}}+\alpha_2 I_{\{\ell\in B\}}+\alpha_3 I_{\{\ell\in C\}}+\varepsilon_\ell .
\]

The group means are

\[
\tau_1=\mu+\alpha_1,\qquad 
\tau_2=\mu+\alpha_2,\qquad 
\tau_3=\mu+\alpha_3.
\]

The vaccine effects relative to control are

\[
\tau_1-\tau_3=\alpha_1-\alpha_3,
\qquad
\tau_2-\tau_3=\alpha_2-\alpha_3.
\]

---

## (2) Model matrix

Stack the observations as

\[
Y=
(Y_{11},\dots,Y_{1n},Y_{21},\dots,Y_{2m},Y_{31},\dots,Y_{3k})^T.
\]

Let

\[
\beta=(\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)^T.
\]

Then \(Y=X\beta+\varepsilon\), where

\[
X=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 1_n & \mathbf 1_n & \mathbf 0_n & \mathbf 0_n\\
\mathbf 1_m & \mathbf 0_m & \mathbf 1_m & \mathbf 0_m\\
\mathbf 1_k & \mathbf 0_k & \mathbf 0_k & \mathbf 1_k
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Equivalently, the rows are

\[
\begin{cases}
(1,1,0,0), & \text{for group A},\\
(1,0,1,0), & \text{for group B},\\
(1,0,0,1), & \text{for control}.
\end{cases}
\]

---

## (3) Can all of \(\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3\) be estimated?

No. The model is not identifiable as written.

The reason is that the intercept column is the sum of the three group-indicator columns:

\[
\mathbf 1_N
=
I_A+I_B+I_C.
\]

Hence the columns of \(X\) are linearly dependent. In fact,

\[
X
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
-1\\
-1\\
-1
\end{pmatrix}
=0.
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=3<4\), so \(X^T X\) is singular and the four parameters are not uniquely estimable.

Indeed, for any constant \(t\),

\[
(\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)
\]

and

\[
(\mu+t,\alpha_1-t,\alpha_2-t,\alpha_3-t)
\]

give the same fitted group means, because

\[
(\mu+t)+(\alpha_i-t)=\mu+\alpha_i.
\]

Therefore \(\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3\) are not individually identifiable. Only the group means \(\mu+\alpha_i\) and contrasts such as \(\alpha_1-\alpha_3\), \(\alpha_2-\alpha_3\) are estimable.

A standard fix is to impose one identifying constraint or to drop one column.

### Fix 1: Use control as reference group

Set the control group as the baseline and write

\[
Y_\ell=\beta_0+\beta_A I_{\{\ell\in A\}}+\beta_B I_{\{\ell\in B\}}+\varepsilon_\ell.
\]

Then the model matrix is

\[
X_{\text{ref}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 1_n & \mathbf 1_n & \mathbf 0_n\\
\mathbf 1_m & \mathbf 0_m & \mathbf 1_m\\
\mathbf 1_k & \mathbf 0_k & \mathbf 0_k
\end{pmatrix},
\]

which has full column rank \(3\). Here

\[
\beta_0=\tau_3,
\qquad
\beta_A=\tau_1-\tau_3,
\qquad
\beta_B=\tau_2-\tau_3.
\]

Thus \(\beta_A\) and \(\beta_B\) are the vaccine effects relative to the control.

The least-squares estimates are

\[
\widehat{\beta}_0=\bar Y_C,
\qquad
\widehat{\beta}_A=\bar Y_A-\bar Y_C,
\qquad
\widehat{\beta}_B=\bar Y_B-\bar Y_C.
\]

### Fix 2: Impose a sum-to-zero constraint

Alternatively, impose for example

\[
\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3=0.
\]

Then \(\mu\) is the average of the three group means, and the parameters become identifiable.

If one wants \(\mu\) to be the sample-size weighted overall mean, then use instead

\[
n\alpha_1+m\alpha_2+k\alpha_3=0.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat{\mu}
=
\frac{n\bar Y_A+m\bar Y_B+k\bar Y_C}{n+m+k},
\]

and

\[
\widehat{\alpha}_1=\bar Y_A-\widehat{\mu},\qquad
\widehat{\alpha}_2=\bar Y_B-\widehat{\mu},\qquad
\widehat{\alpha}_3=\bar Y_C-\widehat{\mu}.
\]

So the original four-parameter model is overparameterized; one must either impose a constraint or use a full-rank reparameterization.
